To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the injured runners engaged in a number of identity work activities in order to sustain a credible sporting identity and momentum towards restitution to full running ability and re‐engaging with their cherished leisure.
identity work was crucial in sustaining a sense of self during long term injury, and in generating the momentum towards the goal to re‐engage with a cherished form leisure.

identity work was a key mechanism for the maintenance of a credible sporting identity during the liminal period of long‐term running injury and rehabilitation, and that this identity work involved the use of three key forms of identification, namely materialistic, associative, and vocabularic, which were deployed in a variety of ways in order to maintain continuity of identity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways that injured athletes manage their identities, and how the disruption of athletic identity is managed.
the ‘working out’ of identity, and with the management of disrupted identity in the context of long‐term athletic injury.
the ‘everyday’ nature of identity, and with the ways in which people actively work to sustain and restore a sense of self‐identity in the face of injury and disruption to their sporting identity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, for the injured participants, ‘working out’ their identities was a vital part of the recovery process.
the two participants’ experiences were very much in accord with those reported by other athletes who have experienced injury.
identity work is an essential and ongoing process in the lives of all athletes, but that it is especially crucial in the face of the threat to the sporting self posed by long‐term injury.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the article contributes to a growing literature on the sociology and social psychology of sport, injury and rehabilitation by examining the impact of long term injury on the identities and identity management strategies of two amateur, but serious middle/ long distance runners.

this study provides a detailed account of the ways in which the identities of two injured runners were managed during the liminality and disruption of injury and rehabilitation, and that this was achieved through a range of identity work practices, which were found to be essential in maintaining a credible and meaningful sporting identity, and in sustaining the motivation to achieve the ultimate goal of full running fitness and a return to running.

the two participants in this study were able to manage their disrupted identity by using a combination of identity work strategies, including materialistic and associative identifications, as well as vocabularic identiﬁcations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
identity is not static and unchanging, but is a process of ongoing construction and reconstruction.

identity work is a crucial element of the recovery process for injured distance runners, and is a key factor in the maintenance of a credible sporting identity and in the generation of momentum towards the goal.
the injured runners’ identities were not simply disrupted by injury; instead, they were actively re‐worked in order to manage and sustain the identity.
